text:
TipHow these exercises work



Each topic starts with a real scenario and a bar model, then three levels of exercises. Level 1 (Guided) fills in the blanks of a finished function. Level 2 (Practice) applies it to new numbers. Level 3 (Challenge) asks a new question with little scaffolding. The R and Python exercises run in your browser: click Run Code to try, Submit Answer to check, and use the hint or solution if you get stuck. Excel exercises have a solution you can reveal.

title: Tracking Spending
text:
Book Topics

Tracking vs. budgeting: tracking records where money actually went; budgeting allocates where it should go; comparing the two creates a feedback loop
Capture methods: spending journal, checkbook register, cash envelopes, bank statements; pick one and run it for a full month
Categorizing: start with about 10 stable buckets (housing, transportation, groceries, dining out, subscriptions, personal, health, gifts, fun money, other); when in doubt use “Other”, and only promote a new category after seeing it three months in a row
Using spreadsheets: bank exports have Date, Description, and Amount columns; a keyword lookup adds the Category column in one pass
Monthly review: pull, categorize, compare to budget, and pick one change for next month
Online subscriptions: Americans spend about $219/month on subscriptions and underestimate it by $133; audit every quarter and cancel anything unused in 30 days
Math: the subscription audit, the opportunity cost of a $20/month subscription invested at 7% for 30 years (about $22,700)

title: Tracking Spending
text:
Categorizing Transactions
A bank export only says where the money went (Description). Adding a Category column turns a list of merchants into budget buckets. In R, dplyr::case_when() checks each rule in order and the first match wins; in Python, numpy.select() does the same with a list of conditions and a list of labels; in Excel, IFS() does it one cell at a time. Anything that matches no rule falls into “Other”.

Level 1: Guided
Fill in the blanks so grocery stores (Trader Joe’s, Whole Foods, Costco) become “Groceries” and everything without a rule becomes “Other”. How many transactions are groceries?

ExcelPythonR


With Description in column B, write an IFS() formula in D2 that labels subscriptions, groceries, and “Other”, then fill it down and count the groceries.






NoteSolution





SEARCH() finds a keyword in a cell, ISNUMBER() turns that into true/false, and OR() joins several keywords. The final TRUE, "Other" catches everything else.
=IFS(
  OR(ISNUMBER(SEARCH("Netflix",B2)),ISNUMBER(SEARCH("Spotify",B2)),ISNUMBER(SEARCH("NYTimes",B2)),ISNUMBER(SEARCH("24 Hour Fitness",B2))), "Subscriptions",
  OR(ISNUMBER(SEARCH("Trader Joe",B2)),ISNUMBER(SEARCH("Whole Foods",B2)),ISNUMBER(SEARCH("Costco",B2))), "Groceries",
  TRUE, "Other"
)



IFS() in Excel


Then count them with =COUNTIF(D:D, "Groceries"). The answer is 3.






#| exercise: cat_1_py
#| setup: true
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
statement = pd.DataFrame({
    "Description": [
        "Employer Payroll", "Rent", "Comcast Internet", "Trader Joe's",
        "Shell Gas", "Netflix", "Starbucks", "PG&E Electric",
        "AT&T Wireless", "Spotify", "Whole Foods", "Chipotle",
        "Geico Auto Insurance", "NYTimes Digital", "Shell Gas", "Costco",
        "24 Hour Fitness"],
    "Amount": [
         2400.00, -1500.00, -75.00, -82.45, -45.20, -15.99, -6.75,
        -142.30, -85.00, -10.99, -64.12, -14.50, -125.00, -17.00,
         -42.80, -156.78, -39.99]
})


#| exercise: cat_1_py
desc = statement["Description"]
statement["Category"] = np.select(
    [desc.str.contains("Netflix|Spotify|NYTimes|24 Hour Fitness"),
     desc.str.contains(______)],
    ["Subscriptions", "Groceries"],
    default=______
)
(statement["Category"] == "Groceries").sum()


Separate the store names with | (it means “or”): "Trader Joe|Whole Foods|Costco". The default label is "Other".


Solution. 
desc = statement["Description"]
statement["Category"] = np.select(
    [desc.str.contains("Netflix|Spotify|NYTimes|24 Hour Fitness"),
     desc.str.contains("Trader Joe|Whole Foods|Costco")],
    ["Subscriptions", "Groceries"],
    default="Other"
)
(statement["Category"] == "Groceries").sum()


#| exercise: cat_1_py
#| check: true
if result == 3:
    feedback = {"correct": True, "message": "Right: Trader Joe's, Whole Foods, and Costco."}
else:
    feedback = {"correct": False, "message": "Not quite. List all three stores, separated by |."}
feedback




#| exercise: cat_1_r
#| setup: true
library(dplyr)
statement <- data.frame(
  Description = c(
    "Employer Payroll", "Rent", "Comcast Internet", "Trader Joe's",
    "Shell Gas", "Netflix", "Starbucks", "PG&E Electric",
    "AT&T Wireless", "Spotify", "Whole Foods", "Chipotle",
    "Geico Auto Insurance", "NYTimes Digital", "Shell Gas", "Costco",
    "24 Hour Fitness"),
  Amount = c(
     2400.00, -1500.00, -75.00, -82.45, -45.20, -15.99, -6.75,
    -142.30, -85.00, -10.99, -64.12, -14.50, -125.00, -17.00,
     -42.80, -156.78, -39.99)
)


#| exercise: cat_1_r
statement |>
  mutate(Category = case_when(
    grepl("Netflix|Spotify|NYTimes|24 Hour Fitness", Description) ~ "Subscriptions",
    grepl(______, Description) ~ "Groceries",
    TRUE ~ ______
  )) |>
  filter(Category == "Groceries") |>
  nrow()


Separate the store names with | (it means “or”): "Trader Joe|Whole Foods|Costco". The last rule’s label is "Other".


Solution. 
statement |>
  mutate(Category = case_when(
    grepl("Netflix|Spotify|NYTimes|24 Hour Fitness", Description) ~ "Subscriptions",
    grepl("Trader Joe|Whole Foods|Costco", Description) ~ "Groceries",
    TRUE ~ "Other"
  )) |>
  filter(Category == "Groceries") |>
  nrow()


#| exercise: cat_1_r
#| check: true
if (isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(.result), 3))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Right: Trader Joe's, Whole Foods, and Costco.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Not quite. List all three stores, separated by |.")
}






Level 2: Practice
Next month’s export has three new merchants: Safeway (groceries), Hulu (a subscription), and Uber (transportation). The rules below don’t know them yet, so they land in “Other”. Update the rules so no transaction is left in “Other”.

ExcelPythonR


Your IFS() formula labels the new month’s Safeway, Hulu, and Uber rows as “Other”. Edit it so =COUNTIF(D:D, "Other") returns 0.






NoteSolution





Add each new merchant to its group with another ISNUMBER(SEARCH(...)) inside the OR(), and add a Transportation rule:
OR(..., ISNUMBER(SEARCH("Safeway",B2))), "Groceries",
OR(..., ISNUMBER(SEARCH("Hulu",B2))), "Subscriptions",
OR(ISNUMBER(SEARCH("Shell",B2)),ISNUMBER(SEARCH("Uber",B2))), "Transportation",
Re-fill the formula down after editing it.






#| exercise: cat_2_py
#| setup: true
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
statement = pd.DataFrame({
    "Description": ["Employer Payroll", "Rent", "Safeway", "Hulu",
                    "Netflix", "Uber Trip", "Shell Gas", "Chipotle"],
    "Amount": [2400.00, -1500.00, -71.20, -17.99, -15.99, -23.40, -44.10, -13.25]
})


#| exercise: cat_2_py
desc = statement["Description"]
statement["Category"] = np.select(
    [desc.str.contains("Payroll"),
     desc.str.contains("Rent"),
     desc.str.contains("Trader Joe|Whole Foods|Costco"),
     desc.str.contains("Netflix|Spotify|NYTimes|24 Hour Fitness"),
     desc.str.contains("Shell"),
     desc.str.contains("Starbucks|Chipotle")],
    ["Income", "Housing", "Groceries", "Subscriptions", "Transportation", "Dining"],
    default="Other"
)
(statement["Category"] == "Other").sum()


Add each new merchant to the pattern for its group, separated by |. For example, "Shell|Uber".


Solution. 
desc = statement["Description"]
statement["Category"] = np.select(
    [desc.str.contains("Payroll"),
     desc.str.contains("Rent"),
     desc.str.contains("Trader Joe|Whole Foods|Costco|Safeway"),
     desc.str.contains("Netflix|Spotify|NYTimes|24 Hour Fitness|Hulu"),
     desc.str.contains("Shell|Uber"),
     desc.str.contains("Starbucks|Chipotle")],
    ["Income", "Housing", "Groceries", "Subscriptions", "Transportation", "Dining"],
    default="Other"
)
(statement["Category"] == "Other").sum()


#| exercise: cat_2_py
#| check: true
if result == 0:
    feedback = {"correct": True, "message": "Right: every transaction has a home."}
else:
    feedback = {"correct": False, "message": f"{result} transaction(s) are still 'Other'. Check Safeway, Hulu, and Uber."}
feedback

#| setup: true
library(dplyr)
statement <- data.frame(
  Description = c("Employer Payroll", "Rent", "Safeway", "Hulu",
                  "Netflix", "Uber Trip", "Shell Gas", "Chipotle"),
  Amount = c(2400.00, -1500.00, -71.20, -17.99, -15.99, -23.40, -44.10, -13.25)
)


#| exercise: cat_2_r
statement |>
  mutate(Category = case_when(
    grepl("Payroll", Description) ~ "Income",
    grepl("Rent", Description) ~ "Housing",
    grepl("Trader Joe|Whole Foods|Costco", Description) ~ "Groceries",
    grepl("Netflix|Spotify|NYTimes|24 Hour Fitness", Description) ~ "Subscriptions",
    grepl("Shell", Description) ~ "Transportation",
    grepl("Starbucks|Chipotle", Description) ~ "Dining",
    TRUE ~ "Other"
  )) |>
  filter(Category == "Other") |>
  nrow()


Add each new merchant to the pattern for its group, separated by |. For example, "Shell|Uber".


Solution. 
statement |>
  mutate(Category = case_when(
    grepl("Payroll", Description) ~ "Income",
    grepl("Rent", Description) ~ "Housing",
    grepl("Trader Joe|Whole Foods|Costco|Safeway", Description) ~ "Groceries",
    grepl("Netflix|Spotify|NYTimes|24 Hour Fitness|Hulu", Description) ~ "Subscriptions",
    grepl("Shell|Uber", Description) ~ "Transportation",
    grepl("Starbucks|Chipotle", Description) ~ "Dining",
    TRUE ~ "Other"
  )) |>
  filter(Category == "Other") |>
  nrow()


#| exercise: cat_2_r
#| check: true
if (isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(.result), 0))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Right: every transaction has a home.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = paste(.result, "transaction(s) are still 'Other'. Check Safeway, Hulu, and Uber."))
}






Level 3: Challenge
Real bank exports are messy: the same merchant can show up as NETFLIX.COM, Netflix, or netflix. The rule below only matches the exact capitalization, so it finds just 1 of the 3 subscriptions. Change the code so capitalization doesn’t matter, and count the subscriptions again.

ExcelPythonR


Does the IFS() and SEARCH() formula need any change for NETFLIX.COM?






NoteSolution





No. SEARCH() ignores capitalization, so SEARCH("Netflix", "NETFLIX.COM") already finds a match. (Its case-sensitive cousin is FIND().)






#| exercise: cat_3_py
#| setup: true
import pandas as pd
messy = pd.DataFrame({
    "Description": ["NETFLIX.COM", "Spotify USA", "nytimes digital",
                    "SHELL OIL 1234", "Whole Foods #102"],
    "Amount": [-15.99, -10.99, -17.00, -45.20, -64.12]
})


#| exercise: cat_3_py
is_sub = messy["Description"].str.contains("Netflix|Spotify|NYTimes|24 Hour Fitness")
is_sub.sum()


str.contains() has a case argument. Look at what case=False does.


Solution. 
is_sub = messy["Description"].str.contains("Netflix|Spotify|NYTimes|24 Hour Fitness", case=False)
is_sub.sum()


#| exercise: cat_3_py
#| check: true
if result == 3:
    feedback = {"correct": True, "message": "Right: all three subscriptions, whatever the capitalization."}
else:
    feedback = {"correct": False, "message": "Not quite. Make the match ignore capitalization."}
feedback




#| exercise: cat_3_r
#| setup: true
library(dplyr)
messy <- data.frame(
  Description = c("NETFLIX.COM", "Spotify USA", "nytimes digital",
                  "SHELL OIL 1234", "Whole Foods #102"),
  Amount = c(-15.99, -10.99, -17.00, -45.20, -64.12)
)


#| exercise: cat_3_r
messy |>
  filter(grepl("Netflix|Spotify|NYTimes|24 Hour Fitness", Description)) |>
  nrow()


grepl() has an ignore.case argument.


Solution. 
messy |>
  filter(grepl("Netflix|Spotify|NYTimes|24 Hour Fitness", Description, ignore.case = TRUE)) |>
  nrow()


#| exercise: cat_3_r
#| check: true
if (isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(.result), 3))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Right: all three subscriptions, whatever the capitalization.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Not quite. Make the match ignore capitalization.")
}

title: Tracking Spending
text:
Answering Tracking Questions
Once every row has a category, the book’s three tracking questions take one short pipeline each: what did subscriptions cost, what share of income went to fixed costs, and which variable category was biggest? Spending is stored as negative numbers, so a minus sign turns a spending total positive.

Level 1: Guided
What did the four subscriptions cost this month?

ExcelPythonR


With Amount in C and Category in D, total the subscriptions as a positive number.






NoteSolution





=-SUMIF(D:D, "Subscriptions", C:C)
This returns $83.97.






#| exercise: q_1_py
#| setup: true
import pandas as pd
statement = pd.DataFrame({
    "Description": [
        "Employer Payroll", "Rent", "Comcast Internet", "Trader Joe's",
        "Shell Gas", "Netflix", "Starbucks", "PG&E Electric",
        "AT&T Wireless", "Spotify", "Whole Foods", "Chipotle",
        "Geico Auto Insurance", "NYTimes Digital", "Shell Gas", "Costco",
        "24 Hour Fitness"],
    "Amount": [
         2400.00, -1500.00, -75.00, -82.45, -45.20, -15.99, -6.75,
        -142.30, -85.00, -10.99, -64.12, -14.50, -125.00, -17.00,
         -42.80, -156.78, -39.99],
    "Category": [
        "Income", "Housing", "Utilities", "Groceries", "Transportation",
        "Subscriptions", "Dining", "Utilities", "Utilities", "Subscriptions",
        "Groceries", "Dining", "Insurance", "Subscriptions", "Transportation",
        "Groceries", "Subscriptions"]
})


#| exercise: q_1_py
-statement.loc[statement["Category"] == ______, "Amount"].sum()


Pick the rows whose Category is "Subscriptions".


Solution. 
-statement.loc[statement["Category"] == "Subscriptions", "Amount"].sum()


#| exercise: q_1_py
#| check: true
if result is not None and abs(result - 83.97) < 0.01:
    feedback = {"correct": True, "message": "Right: $83.97 a month."}
else:
    feedback = {"correct": False, "message": "Not quite. Filter to Subscriptions and keep the minus sign."}
feedback




#| exercise: q_1_r
#| setup: true
library(dplyr)
statement <- data.frame(
  Description = c(
    "Employer Payroll", "Rent", "Comcast Internet", "Trader Joe's",
    "Shell Gas", "Netflix", "Starbucks", "PG&E Electric",
    "AT&T Wireless", "Spotify", "Whole Foods", "Chipotle",
    "Geico Auto Insurance", "NYTimes Digital", "Shell Gas", "Costco",
    "24 Hour Fitness"),
  Amount = c(
     2400.00, -1500.00, -75.00, -82.45, -45.20, -15.99, -6.75,
    -142.30, -85.00, -10.99, -64.12, -14.50, -125.00, -17.00,
     -42.80, -156.78, -39.99),
  Category = c(
    "Income", "Housing", "Utilities", "Groceries", "Transportation",
    "Subscriptions", "Dining", "Utilities", "Utilities", "Subscriptions",
    "Groceries", "Dining", "Insurance", "Subscriptions", "Transportation",
    "Groceries", "Subscriptions")
)


#| exercise: q_1_r
statement |>
  filter(Category == ______) |>
  summarise(total = -sum(Amount)) |>
  pull(total)


Keep the rows whose Category is "Subscriptions".


Solution. 
statement |>
  filter(Category == "Subscriptions") |>
  summarise(total = -sum(Amount)) |>
  pull(total)


#| exercise: q_1_r
#| check: true
if (isTRUE(all.equal(.result, 83.97))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Right: $83.97 a month.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Not quite. Filter to Subscriptions and keep the minus sign.")
}






Level 2: Practice
Fixed costs are housing, utilities, and insurance. What share of income went to fixed costs? Give the answer as a decimal (for example, 0.25 for 25%).

ExcelPythonR


Total the three fixed categories and divide by income (the positive amounts).






NoteSolution





=-(SUMIF(D:D,"Housing",C:C)+SUMIF(D:D,"Utilities",C:C)+SUMIF(D:D,"Insurance",C:C))/SUMIF(C:C,">0")
This returns 0.803, or about 80%.






#| exercise: q_2_py
#| setup: true
import pandas as pd
statement = pd.DataFrame({
    "Amount": [
         2400.00, -1500.00, -75.00, -82.45, -45.20, -15.99, -6.75,
        -142.30, -85.00, -10.99, -64.12, -14.50, -125.00, -17.00,
         -42.80, -156.78, -39.99],
    "Category": [
        "Income", "Housing", "Utilities", "Groceries", "Transportation",
        "Subscriptions", "Dining", "Utilities", "Utilities", "Subscriptions",
        "Groceries", "Dining", "Insurance", "Subscriptions", "Transportation",
        "Groceries", "Subscriptions"]
})


#| exercise: q_2_py
fixed = ["Housing", "Utilities", "Insurance"]
income = statement.loc[statement["Amount"] > 0, "Amount"].sum()
fixed_total = ______
fixed_total / income


statement["Category"].isin(fixed) picks the fixed-cost rows. Sum their Amount and flip the sign.


Solution. 
fixed = ["Housing", "Utilities", "Insurance"]
income = statement.loc[statement["Amount"] > 0, "Amount"].sum()
fixed_total = -statement.loc[statement["Category"].isin(fixed), "Amount"].sum()
fixed_total / income


#| exercise: q_2_py
#| check: true
if result is not None and abs(result - 0.8030) < 0.001:
    feedback = {"correct": True, "message": "Right: about 80%. This statement has the full month's rent but only one paycheck."}
else:
    feedback = {"correct": False, "message": "Not quite. Total housing, utilities, and insurance as a positive number."}
feedback




#| exercise: q_2_r
#| setup: true
library(dplyr)
statement <- data.frame(
  Amount = c(
     2400.00, -1500.00, -75.00, -82.45, -45.20, -15.99, -6.75,
    -142.30, -85.00, -10.99, -64.12, -14.50, -125.00, -17.00,
     -42.80, -156.78, -39.99),
  Category = c(
    "Income", "Housing", "Utilities", "Groceries", "Transportation",
    "Subscriptions", "Dining", "Utilities", "Utilities", "Subscriptions",
    "Groceries", "Dining", "Insurance", "Subscriptions", "Transportation",
    "Groceries", "Subscriptions")
)


#| exercise: q_2_r
fixed <- c("Housing", "Utilities", "Insurance")
income <- statement |> filter(Amount > 0) |> pull(Amount) |> sum()
fixed_total <- ______
fixed_total / income


filter(Category %in% fixed) keeps the fixed-cost rows; then summarise(total = -sum(Amount)) and pull(total).


Solution. 
fixed <- c("Housing", "Utilities", "Insurance")
income <- statement |> filter(Amount > 0) |> pull(Amount) |> sum()
fixed_total <- statement |> filter(Category %in% fixed) |> summarise(total = -sum(Amount)) |> pull(total)
fixed_total / income


#| exercise: q_2_r
#| check: true
if (isTRUE(all.equal(.result, 0.8030417, tolerance = 1e-4))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Right: about 80%. This statement has the full month's rent but only one paycheck.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Not quite. Total housing, utilities, and insurance as a positive number.")
}






Level 3: Challenge
Leaving out income, fixed costs, and subscriptions, which category had the most spending? Return its name.

ExcelPythonR


Find the biggest variable category without scrolling through the rows.






NoteSolution





Select the data and use Insert → PivotTable with Category in Rows and Amount in Values, then sort smallest to largest (spending is negative). Or list the variable categories in F2:F4 (Groceries, Transportation, Dining), total each in G2 with =-SUMIF(D:D, F2, C:C), fill down, and use:
=INDEX(F2:F4, MATCH(MAX(G2:G4), G2:G4, 0))
The answer is Groceries ($303.35).

#| setup: true
import pandas as pd
statement = pd.DataFrame({
    "Amount": [
         2400.00, -1500.00, -75.00, -82.45, -45.20, -15.99, -6.75,
        -142.30, -85.00, -10.99, -64.12, -14.50, -125.00, -17.00,
         -42.80, -156.78, -39.99],
    "Category": [
        "Income", "Housing", "Utilities", "Groceries", "Transportation",
        "Subscriptions", "Dining", "Utilities", "Utilities", "Subscriptions",
        "Groceries", "Dining", "Insurance", "Subscriptions", "Transportation",
        "Groceries", "Subscriptions"]
})


#| exercise: q_3_py
skip = ["Income", "Housing", "Utilities", "Insurance", "Subscriptions"]
# total spending by category, then return the name of the biggest



Filter out the skip categories with ~statement["Category"].isin(skip), then groupby("Category")["Amount"].sum(). Spending is negative, so the biggest is .idxmin().


Solution. 
skip = ["Income", "Housing", "Utilities", "Insurance", "Subscriptions"]
variable = statement[~statement["Category"].isin(skip)]
variable.groupby("Category")["Amount"].sum().idxmin()


#| exercise: q_3_py
#| check: true
if result == "Groceries":
    feedback = {"correct": True, "message": "Right: Groceries, at $303.35."}
else:
    feedback = {"correct": False, "message": "Not quite. Spending is negative, so the biggest total is the most negative."}
feedback

#| setup: true
library(dplyr)
statement <- data.frame(
  Amount = c(
     2400.00, -1500.00, -75.00, -82.45, -45.20, -15.99, -6.75,
    -142.30, -85.00, -10.99, -64.12, -14.50, -125.00, -17.00,
     -42.80, -156.78, -39.99),
  Category = c(
    "Income", "Housing", "Utilities", "Groceries", "Transportation",
    "Subscriptions", "Dining", "Utilities", "Utilities", "Subscriptions",
    "Groceries", "Dining", "Insurance", "Subscriptions", "Transportation",
    "Groceries", "Subscriptions")
)


#| exercise: q_3_r
skip <- c("Income", "Housing", "Utilities", "Insurance", "Subscriptions")
# total spending by category, then return the name of the biggest



filter(!Category %in% skip), then group_by(Category) and summarise(Total = -sum(Amount)). Finish with slice_max(Total, n = 1) and pull(Category).


Solution. 
skip <- c("Income", "Housing", "Utilities", "Insurance", "Subscriptions")
statement |>
  filter(!Category %in% skip) |>
  group_by(Category) |>
  summarise(Total = -sum(Amount)) |>
  slice_max(Total, n = 1) |>
  pull(Category)


#| exercise: q_3_r
#| check: true
if (identical(as.character(.result), "Groceries")) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Right: Groceries, at $303.35.")
} else {

}

title: Tracking Spending
Getting set up
text:
The exercises on this site are written in two free programming languages: R and Python. You don’t need to know either one yet—this page walks you through installing both, no matter which computer you use.
A few words you’ll see along the way:

title: Getting set up
text:
Installing R
R is the language I’m most familiar with, so we will install it first. We’ll install two things: R itself (the engine) and RStudio (the workspace where you’ll actually write code).

Step 1 — Install R
Pick the tab for your computer below.

WindowsmacOSLinux



Go to the R download page: cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/base.
Click the large Download R for Windows link at the top.
Open the file you just downloaded (it’ll be in your Downloads folder).
Click Next through the installer, accepting the suggested options.




Go to the R download page: cran.r-project.org/bin/macosx.
Download the file that matches your Mac:

Apple Silicon (M1, M2, M3, or newer) — most Macs sold since late 2020.
Intel — older Macs.
Not sure? Click the Apple menu () in the top-left corner → About This Mac. If it says “Apple M…”, choose Apple Silicon.

Open the downloaded .pkg file and click Continue through the installer.



Most Linux systems install R through their built-in software manager. Open a terminal and run the command for your system:
On Ubuntu, Pop!_OS, or Debian:
sudo apt update && sudo apt install r-base
On Fedora:
sudo dnf install R





Step 2 — Install RStudio
RStudio is the same on every operating system.

Go to posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop.
Scroll to Step 2 on that page and click the download button for your computer (the website detects it for you).
Open the downloaded file and follow the prompts to install.







Note



Install R before RStudio. RStudio is just the workspace—it needs R already on your computer to do anything.




Step 3 — Check that R works
Open RStudio. In the Console (the panel on the left), type the line below and press Enter:
2 + 2
If you see [1] 4, R is working. 🎉

title: Getting set up
text:
Installing Python
Python is the second language we’ll use. We’ll install Python itself and a free workspace called Positron.

Step 1 — Install Python

WindowsmacOSLinux



Go to python.org/downloads and click the yellow Download Python button.
Open the downloaded file.
Important: on the first installer screen, check the box that says Add Python to PATH before clicking Install Now. This lets your computer find Python later.




Go to python.org/downloads and click the yellow Download Python button.
Open the downloaded .pkg file and click Continue through the installer, accepting the suggested options.



Most Linux systems already include Python. Open a terminal and run the command for your system to make sure it’s installed:
On Ubuntu, Pop!_OS, or Debian:
sudo apt update && sudo apt install python3 python3-pip
On Fedora:
sudo dnf install python3 python3-pip





Step 2 — Install Positron
Positron is a free workspace for writing Python (and R) code, made by the same team as RStudio.

Go to positron.posit.co/download.
Download the version for your computer.
Open the downloaded file and follow the prompts to install.



Step 3 — Check that Python works
Open a console and type the line below, then press Enter:

WindowsmacOS / Linux


Open the Start menu, type cmd, and open Command Prompt. Then run:
python --version


Open the Terminal app and run:
python3 --version



If you see something like Python 3.12.0, Python is working. 🎉

title: Retirement Accounts
text:
Book Topics

What a retirement account is: a container, not an investment; it decides how the investments inside get taxed; early withdrawals before 59 and a half usually cost a 10% penalty plus income tax
2026 limits: 401(k)/403(b)/TSP $24,500; Traditional and Roth IRA $7,500 (one shared limit); HSA $4,400 (self); taxable brokerage has no limit
The plan at work: contributions come out of each paycheck; a common match is “50% of the first 6%”; watch vesting and don’t settle for the automatic enrollment rate
Traditional vs. Roth: pay tax later or pay it now; the only thing that matters is whether your tax rate is lower now or later, so Roth is the usual default early in a career
The IRA: opened at a brokerage, yours no matter where you work; Roth contributions (not earnings) can come out any time; Roth income limit is $153,000 to $168,000 (single)
The HSA: needs an HSA eligible (high deductible) plan; tax free going in, growing, and coming out for medical costs
Which account first: deductible cash, full match, high interest debt, emergency fund, HSA and Roth IRA, more 401(k), then taxable; aim for 15% of income including the match
Changing jobs: roll the old plan over directly; cashing out $5,000 at 22 leaves about $3,900 instead of about $100,000 by 67

title: Retirement Accounts
text:
The Employer Match
Your employer adds money on top of what you put in, up to a limit.
Formula: Match = Salary × min(Your %, Match limit %) × Match rate
Example: $45,000 × min(6%, 6%) × 50% = $1,350 a year in free money. At 3%, you’d only get $675.





6% of a $45,000 salary, plus a 50% employer match







6% of a $45,000 salary, plus a 50% employer match




The second example runs the same job across several contribution rates. Past 6%, your own deposits keep growing but the match stops. The last example shows what one year of the full match becomes if it stays invested for 40 years at 7%.
Read the match as a 50% return the day you deposit. Contributing 3% instead of 6% leaves $675 a year on the table, and one year of the full match grows to about $20,200 over 40 years at 7%.

Level 1: Guided
Fill in the blanks to finish employer_match(), then find the yearly match on a $45,000 salary when you contribute 6% and the employer matches 50% of the first 6%.

ExcelPythonR


Put the salary in A2 (45000), your contribution in B2 (0.06), the match limit in C2 (0.06), and the match rate in D2 (0.5). Find the match in E2.






NoteSolution





=A2 * MIN(B2, C2) * D2
This returns $1,350.






#| exercise: match_1_py
def employer_match(salary, contribution_pct, match_limit_pct, match_rate):
    return salary * ______(contribution_pct, match_limit_pct) * match_rate

employer_match(45000, 0.06, 0.06, 0.50)


The employer only matches up to the limit, so use the smaller of your % and the limit.


Solution. 
def employer_match(salary, contribution_pct, match_limit_pct, match_rate):
    return salary * min(contribution_pct, match_limit_pct) * match_rate

employer_match(45000, 0.06, 0.06, 0.50)


#| exercise: match_1_py
#| check: true
if result is not None and abs(result - 1350) < 0.01:
    feedback = {"correct": True, "message": "Right: $1,350 a year of free money."}
else:
    feedback = {"correct": False, "message": "Not quite. Use the smaller of your % and the limit."}
feedback




#| exercise: match_1_r
employer_match <- function(salary, contribution_pct, match_limit_pct, match_rate) {
  salary * ______(contribution_pct, match_limit_pct) * match_rate
}
employer_match(45000, 0.06, 0.06, 0.50)


The employer only matches up to the limit, so use the smaller of your % and the limit. pmin() does it element by element.


Solution. 
employer_match <- function(salary, contribution_pct, match_limit_pct, match_rate) {
  salary * pmin(contribution_pct, match_limit_pct) * match_rate
}
employer_match(45000, 0.06, 0.06, 0.50)


#| exercise: match_1_r
#| check: true
if (isTRUE(abs(as.numeric(.result) - 1350) < 0.01)) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Right: $1,350 a year of free money.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Not quite. Use the smaller of your % and the limit.")
}

NoteSolution

Level 3: Challenge
Five coworkers each earn $45,000 with the same 50%-of-6% match, contributing 0%, 3%, 6%, 10%, and 15%. The full match is $1,350. How much match do they miss in total?

ExcelPythonR


Put the rates in A2:A6, the match in B, and the missed match in C, then total it.






NoteSolution





In B2, filled down: =45000*MIN(A2, 6%)*50%. In C2: =1350 - B2. Then =SUM(C2:C6) returns $2,025. Contributing more than 6% doesn’t earn more match.

coworkers = pd.DataFrame({"pct": [0, 0.03, 0.06, 0.10, 0.15]})


#| exercise: match_3_py

Solution.

(1350 - coworkers["match"]).sum()

    feedback = {"correct": True, "message": "Right: $2,025 missed, all by the two who contribute under 6%."}
else:
    feedback = {"correct": False, "message": "Not quite. Cap each rate at 6% before computing the match."}
feedback

library(dplyr)
employer_match <- function(salary, contribution_pct, match_limit_pct, match_rate) {
  salary * pmin(contribution_pct, match_limit_pct) * match_rate
}
coworkers <- data.frame(pct = c(0, 0.03, 0.06, 0.10, 0.15))


#| exercise: match_3_r
# add a match column, then total the missed match


employer_match() uses pmin(), so it works on the whole pct column. Then summarise(missed = sum(1350 - match)).


Solution.

  mutate(match = employer_match(45000, pct, 0.06, 0.50)) |>
  summarise(missed = sum(1350 - match)) |>
  pull(missed)


#| exercise: match_3_r
#| check: true

} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Not quite. Cap each rate at 6% before computing the match.")
}

title: Retirement Accounts
text:
Traditional vs. Roth
Roth takes the tax out first, then the rest grows. Traditional lets the whole amount grow, then takes the tax out at the end.
Formula: Amount you keep = Contribution × (1 − tax rate) × (1 + r)^n
For Roth, use today’s tax rate. For Traditional, use your tax rate in retirement.
Example: $1,000 for 40 years at 7%. With 12% now and 12% later, both accounts leave you about $13,178. If your rate in retirement is 22% instead, the Traditional account leaves you about $11,680.





$1,000 after 40 years at 7%, with a 12% tax rate now and later







$1,000 after 40 years at 7%, with a 12% tax rate now and later




Multiplying by (1 − tax rate) gives the same answer whether you do it first or last. So the second example holds today’s rate at 12% and tries several retirement rates. The edge case is a retirement rate lower than today’s, where Traditional wins.
Read the result as a contest between two tax rates. Growth and years don’t pick the winner. Roth wins when today’s rate is lower than your rate in retirement, and Traditional wins when it’s higher.

Level 1: Guided
Fill in the blanks to finish after_tax_value(), then find what $1,000 in a Roth leaves you after 40 years at 7%, taxed at today’s 12% rate.

ExcelPythonR


Put the contribution in A2 (1000), the tax rate in B2 (0.12), the return in C2 (0.07), and years in D2 (40). Find the after-tax value in E2.






NoteSolution





=A2 * (1 - B2) * (1 + C2)^D2
This returns $13,177.52.






#| exercise: roth_1_py
def after_tax_value(contribution, tax_rate, rate, years):
    return contribution * (1 - ______) * (1 + rate) ** ______

after_tax_value(1000, 0.12, 0.07, 40)


Taxes take a share of the money; growth multiplies it once per year.


Solution. 
def after_tax_value(contribution, tax_rate, rate, years):
    return contribution * (1 - tax_rate) * (1 + rate) ** years

after_tax_value(1000, 0.12, 0.07, 40)


#| exercise: roth_1_py
#| check: true
if result is not None and abs(result - 13177.522899) < 0.01:
    feedback = {"correct": True, "message": "Right: about $13,178 you keep."}
else:

feedback

Write a small function that compares roth with after_tax_value(1000, r, 0.07, 40), checking the tie first, and use a list comprehension.

        return "tie"
    return "Roth" if roth > trad else "Traditional"

after_tax_value <- function(contribution, tax_rate, rate, years) {

#| exercise: roth_3_r
roth <- after_tax_value(1000, 0.12, 0.07, 40)
later <- c(0.10, 0.12, 0.22, 0.24)
# one label per retirement rate

trad <- after_tax_value(1000, later, 0.07, 40)
case_when(
  abs(roth - trad) < 1 ~ "tie",
  roth > trad ~ "Roth",
  .default = "Traditional"
)


#| exercise: roth_3_r
#| check: true
if (identical(as.character(.result), c("Traditional", "tie", "Roth", "Roth"))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Right: the account taxed at the lower rate wins; equal rates tie.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Not quite. Check for the tie first, then compare the two values.")
}

text:
TipHow these exercises work



Each topic starts with a real scenario and a bar model, then three levels of exercises. Level 1 (Guided) fills in the blanks of a finished function. Level 2 (Practice) applies it to new numbers. Level 3 (Challenge) asks a new question with little scaffolding. title: Managing Debt
text:
Book Topics

Debt hierarchy: every debt has a price (its APR); toxic debt (15 to 29% APR: credit cards, payday loans) gets attacked first, moderate debt (5 to 10%: car loans, private student loans) gets paid down steadily, and strategic debt (3 to 7%: mortgages, federal student loans) gets paid on schedule
Credit cards: pay them off before nearly every other goal (except insurance deductibles and an employer match); the playbook is stop using them, negotiate the APR, pick avalanche or snowball, consider a 0% transfer or cheaper loan, and automate minimums; once paid in full monthly, use cards as a payment tool
Student loans: the return depends on the income premium the degree creates; the 1× rule caps total debt at your expected first year salary, which works out to roughly 14% of gross pay on a standard 10 year plan at 6.5%
Federal IDR plans: payments are a share of discretionary income (AGI minus a multiple of the poverty guideline); SAVE ended in March 2026, RAP starts July 2026 (1 to 10% of AGI, 30 years), IBR is the stable fallback, and PSLF forgives the rest after 10 years of public service
Pay off vs. invest: compare the loan rate to your expected after tax return (above 6% pay off, 4 to 6% do both, below 4% invest), then add a peace of mind premium
Car loans: depreciating assets financed at 7 to 9%; buy used, pay cash, keep loans under 36 months, follow the 20/4/10 rule
Debt and the FOO: high interest debt is step 3, low interest debt is step 9; moderate debt sits in between, after emergency reserves

title: Managing Debt
text:
APR vs. APY
Lenders quote the APR. You actually pay the APY, which is higher because interest compounds.
Formula: APY = (1 + APR ÷ n)^n − 1, where n is the number of compounding periods per year
Example: a 24% APR compounded daily is about 27.1% APY. On a $10,000 balance that is an extra $310 a year.





APR cost vs. APY cost on a $10,000 balance (24% APR, daily compounding)

title: Managing Debt
text:
Minimum Payments
Minimum payments barely touch the balance. Most of each payment goes to interest. As the balance falls, a little more of each payment goes to principal, and the formula accounts for that.
Formula: Months to pay off = −ln(1 − r × Balance ÷ Payment) ÷ ln(1 + r), where r = APR ÷ 12
Example: $5,000 at 22% APR, paying $100 a month. The first month’s interest is about $92, so only $8 reduces the balance. Payoff takes about 137 months (11 years), and you pay about $13,700 in total.





Where a $100 minimum payment actually goes







Where a $100 minimum payment actually goes




The formula only works when the payment is bigger than the first month’s interest. If it isn’t, the balance never shrinks, and the answer comes back as NaN (not a number). Small increases in the payment cut years off the debt.

title: Managing Debt
section: Total Interest Over a Loan’s Life
text:
Total Interest Over a Loan’s Life
For any installment loan (car, mortgage, student loan), the real cost is everything you pay minus what you borrowed.
Formula: Total Interest = (Monthly Payment × Number of Payments) − Loan Principal
Example: a $30,000 car loan at 7%. Over 6 years ($512 a month) you pay $6,864 in interest. Over 4 years ($719 a month) you pay $4,512. The shorter term saves $2,352.

$30,000 car loan: principal vs. interest for 6-year and 4-year terms

title: Managing Debt
section: Student Loan to Income & Standard Payment
text:
Student Loan to Income & Standard Payment
The 1× rule says your student loans should not be bigger than your expected first year salary. Two numbers check it: the loan to income ratio, and the monthly payment that loan creates on a standard 10 year plan.
Formula: Loan to income ratio = Total loans ÷ Expected salary, and Monthly payment = Loan × r(1 + r)^n ÷ ((1 + r)^n − 1), where r = yearly rate ÷ 12 and n = 120 payments
Example: $45,000 ÷ $42,000 = about 1.07×, and the standard payment at 6.5% is about $511 a month.





$45,000 in student loans vs. a $42,000 starting salary







$45,000 in student loans vs. a $42,000 starting salary




A ratio above 1.0 means the loan bar runs past the salary line. At exactly 1×, every dollar borrowed costs about $0.0114 a month, so the payment is about 14% of gross pay no matter the major. What changes is how many dollars are left over.

title: Managing Debt
text:
Income Driven Repayment Monthly Payment
Federal IDR plans protect part of your income and charge a percentage of the rest (your discretionary income).
Formula: Monthly payment = (AGI − threshold × Federal Poverty Guideline) × payment rate ÷ 12
Example (IBR): ($50,000 − 1.5 × $15,650) × 10% ÷ 12 = about $221 a month. For IBR loans from before July 2014 (15% rate), it is about $332.





$50,000 AGI under IBR: protected income, discretionary income, and the yearly payment







$50,000 AGI under IBR: protected income, discretionary income, and the yearly payment




If your AGI is below the protected amount, the payment is $0. Each extra $1,000 of income above that line adds only about $8 a month under IBR. SAVE used the same formula with a 225% threshold and a 5% undergraduate rate, but it ended in March 2026. RAP uses a sliding share of total AGI instead, so this function does not cover it.

title: Managing Debt
text:
Debt to Income Ratio (DTI)
Lenders calculate this about you. Calculate it yourself first.
Formula: DTI = (Total Monthly Debt Payments ÷ Gross Monthly Income) × 100
Example: $2,500 in debt payments on $7,000 gross income is about 36% DTI.
Benchmarks: below 20% healthy; 20 to 35% manageable; 36 to 43% stretched; above 43% danger zone (most mortgage lenders say no).





$7,000 monthly income split into debt payments and remaining income







$7,000 monthly income split into debt payments and remaining income

Managing Debt
text:
Avalanche vs. Snowball Math
Two ways to order several debts. Avalanche pays the highest APR first and saves the most. Snowball pays the smallest balance first and builds momentum.
Formula: Monthly interest saved by an extra payment = Extra payment × APR ÷ 12
Example: an extra $100 on Card B (24%) saves $2.00 of interest next month. The same $100 on Card A (18%) saves $1.50.





Avalanche order (highest APR first) vs. snowball order (smallest balance first)







Avalanche order (highest APR first) vs. snowball order (smallest balance first)




The book says to find the cost of snowball with a payoff calculator. The extra code below is a small one. It pays every minimum, sends the rest of a fixed monthly budget to the target debt, and rolls each freed up payment onto the next debt. The difference in total interest is the price of the snowball’s quick early wins. With these three cards, snowball costs about $338 more and takes one extra month.

This returns Card B (24%).

ExcelPythonR


This one needs a month-by-month table. Build columns for each card’s balance, interest, and payment for 26 rows, or skip to the Python or R tab.






NoteSolution





The avalanche pays $1,782.34 of interest over 25 months and the snowball $2,120.62 over 26, so the snowball costs $338.28 more.






#| exercise: avalanche_3_py
#| setup: true
def order_avalanche(debts):
    return sorted(debts, key=lambda d: d["apr"], reverse=True)

def order_snowball(debts):
    return sorted(debts, key=lambda d: d["balance"])

def payoff_sim(debts, budget, order_fn):
    d = order_fn(debts)
    bal = [x["balance"] for x in d]
    months, interest = 0, 0.0
    while any(b > 0.005 for b in bal):
        months += 1
        for i, x in enumerate(d):
            int_i = bal[i] * x["apr"] / 12
            interest += int_i
            bal[i] += int_i
        pay = [min(x["min_pay"], b) for x, b in zip(d, bal)]
        bal = [b - p for b, p in zip(bal, pay)]
        extra = budget - sum(pay)
        for i in range(len(bal)):
            amt = min(extra, bal[i])
            bal[i] -= amt
            extra -= amt
    return {"months": months, "interest": round(interest, 2)}

]

payoff_sim <- function(debts, budget, order_fn) {
  d <- order_fn(debts)
  bal <- d$balance
  months <- 0
  interest <- 0
  while (any(bal > 0.005)) {
    months   <- months + 1
    int      <- bal * d$apr / 12
    interest <- interest + sum(int)
    bal      <- bal + int
    pay      <- pmin(d$min_pay, bal)
    bal      <- bal - pay
    extra    <- budget - sum(pay)
    for (i in seq_along(bal)) {
      x      <- min(extra, bal[i])
      bal[i] <- bal[i] - x
      extra  <- extra - x
    }
  }
  c(months = months, interest = round(interest, 2))
}

title: Investing Basics
text:
Book Topics

Compounding: interest earning interest; the Rule of 72 says years to double ≈ 72 ÷ annual return % (about 10 years at 7%, about 7 years at 10%); $10,000 at 7% for 40 years
The core portfolio: stocks (70 to 90% with 20+ years), bonds (10 to 30%), and cash (the emergency fund, kept separate); a simple default is 80% total stock market and 20% total bond market index funds, rebalanced once a year for about 0.03% in fees
Risk vs. return: 100% stocks might average 10% but drop 40% in a bad year; 60/40 averages about 7% and drops about 20%; pick the split you can stick with through a bear market
Diversification: one dollar in a total market fund owns thousands of companies, so one failure barely matters
Tax-advantaged accounts: 2026 limits for the 401(k)/403(b) ($24,500), Roth and Traditional IRA ($7,500), HSA ($4,400 self), and taxable accounts; fill them in order (401(k) to the match, Roth IRA or HSA, max the 401(k), then taxable); $10,000 at 7% for 30 years grows to about $76,000, saving about $13,200 in taxes in a Roth
Common mistakes: timing the market, chasing past performance, paying high fees (1% over 30 years costs about 25%), holding too much cash, and selling in a panic

text:
Future Value and the Rule of 72
Each year’s growth is applied to a bigger base, so the balance curves upward instead of rising in a straight line.
Formula: FV = PV × (1 + r)^n
Rule of 72: Years to double ≈ 72 ÷ annual return %
Example: $10,000 at 7% for 10 years grows to about $19,672, and at 7% money doubles roughly every 10 years.





$10,000 growing at 7%: value at each checkpoint







$10,000 growing at 7%: value at each checkpoint




The Rule of 72 is a shortcut. The exact doubling time is log(2) ÷ log(1 + r). The shortcut is very close for returns between about 4% and 12%, and drifts further off at the extremes.
Read the result as “what one deposit becomes if you leave it alone.” At 7%, the Rule of 72 says 10.3 years and the exact answer is 10.2 years, so the shortcut is good enough for planning.

    return present_value * (1 + rate) ** years

title: Investing Basics
text:
Future Value of Regular Contributions
Investing a fixed amount every month builds wealth two ways: the money you put in, and the growth on everything you put in before.
Formula: FV = PMT × [((1 + r)^n − 1) ÷ r]
Example: $500/month for 30 years (360 months) at a 7% annual return (about 0.583% per month) grows to about $610,000, and only $180,000 of that is money you put in.





$500/month contributions at 7%: contributed vs. gains







$500/month contributions at 7%: contributed vs. gains




Starting earlier matters more than putting in more. The second example compares the same $500/month started at 25, 35, and 45, all ending at 65. The book’s recap number ($50/month for 30 years is about $61,000) is the same math at one tenth the size.
Read the result as two layers. At 30 years, about 70% of the $610,000 is growth, not deposits. Starting at 25 instead of 45 more than quadruples the ending balance while only doubling what you put in.

title: Investing Basics
text:
Real (Inflation-Adjusted) Return
Inflation shrinks what each dollar buys, so the return that matters is what’s left after inflation.
Formula: Real Return = (1 + nominal) ÷ (1 + inflation) − 1
Example: (1.07 ÷ 1.03) − 1 = about 3.88%, a little less than the 4% you’d get by simple subtraction.





Nominal return, inflation, and real return







Nominal return, inflation, and real return




The second example compares several investments against 3% inflation. Cash earning 4% (one of the book’s common mistakes) barely beats inflation, and cash earning less than inflation has a negative real return. The last line shows what $76,123 (the book’s 30 year example) is worth in today’s dollars.
Read a negative real return as “losing buying power, even though the balance went up.” The $76,123 in 30 years buys about what $31,400 buys today, which is why the book says to think in real terms.

TipHow these exercises work

title: Index Funds
text:
Book Topics

What an index fund is: an index is a list of companies (like the S&P 500); an index fund buys everything on the list, weighted by company size (market cap), with no manager picking winners (passive vs. active)
Why index funds win: SPIVA shows 79% of large US active funds trailed the S&P 500 in 2025 and about 9 in 10 over 15 years; Bogle’s math says the average investor earns the market return minus costs
Expense ratios: a yearly fee taken out quietly; 0.04% vs. 1% is $4 vs. $100 on $10,000; look for funds under 0.10%
Total market vs. S&P 500 vs. international: the first two move almost together; experts disagree on how much international to hold (Bogle and Collins little or none, Felix anywhere from 10% to 60% home country)
ETFs vs. mutual funds: same holdings, different packaging; ETFs trade all day and are a little more tax efficient, mutual funds make automatic investing easier
How to pick one: go broad, check the expense ratio, look for “index” in the 401(k) list (or a target date fund), automate, and leave it alone

title: Index Funds
text:
The Fee This Year
Every year, the fund takes a slice of your balance as its fee.
Formula: Yearly fee = Balance × Expense ratio
Example: $10,000 × 0.0004 = $4. $10,000 × 0.01 = $100, or 25 times as much.





One year of fees on $10,000







One year of fees on $10,000




The second example uses a table of typical expense ratios across a few balances. The fee grows with your balance, so a fee that costs pocket change at $10,000 costs real money at $250,000.
Read the fee as dollars you never see. The active fund costs $2,500 a year on $250,000, and the index fund costs $100.

title: Index Funds
section: What Fees Cost Over a Lifetime
text:
What Fees Cost Over a Lifetime
The fee comes out of the return, so subtract it from the return before you compound.
Formula: FV = PMT × [((1 + r)^n − 1) ÷ r], where r = (return − expense ratio) ÷ 12
Example: $300/month for 40 years at 7%. The index fund (0.04%) grows to about $778,655 and the active fund (1%) to about $597,447. Both people put in the same $144,000. The 1% fee cost $181,207, about 23% of what the index fund investor ended up with.





$300/month at 7%, with a 0.04% fee vs. a 1% fee







$300/month at 7%, with a 0.04% fee vs. a 1% fee




The second example tries several expense ratios over 40 years and reports the share of the low cost result each one loses. The edge case is a 0% fee, which is just the plain annuity from Investing Basics.
Read the lifetime cost as a share, not a dollar amount. A 1% fee takes about 23% of the ending balance, which is why the book says close to a quarter. A negative “lost” number means that fund beat the 0.04% index fund (only possible here with a lower fee).

This returns $778,654.71.

title: Income
text:
Book Topics

Take-home pay: your salary (gross pay) is not what lands in your account; taxes, Social Security and Medicare (7.65%), 401(k), and health plans come out first, so plan around take-home pay
Wealth vs. spending: true wealth is the income you didn’t spend, quietly compounding (Housel); conspicuous consumption is negatively correlated with actual wealth (Felix)
Human capital: early in a career, future earning potential is the biggest asset; invest in skills and career growth, and take more stock market risk when young (Felix)
Spending and happiness: experiences beat possessions; buying time is a high return use of money; lifestyle inflation is the silent killer; housing is the biggest lever
Three anchoring rules: spend on what you love, cut what you don’t (Sethi); build a gap between ego and income (Housel); keep it simple (Bogle)
Wealth formula: Wealth = Focus + (Stoicism × Time × Diversification); focus is additive, the other three multiply, so a zero on any one collapses the second term (Galloway)
As income grows: split every raise, 50% to investing and 50% to lifestyle
Math: the wealth formula as yearly savings compounding ($62,400 income, 15% saved, 8% for 40 years), the fixed-cost ratio ($1,760 of $3,200 take-home pay, under a 60% ceiling), and what a raise is really worth ($200/month at 7% for 25 years)

text:
Number Formatting
Before working through the math, it helps to have two small formatting utilities that handle the $ and % symbols seen throughout the book. They take a plain number and return a reader-friendly string.

ExcelPythonR


In Excel, number formatting is applied through the toolbar. Select the cells to format and choose the appropriate option from the Number Format dropdown.



Common number formats in Excel


There are two options for money: Currency and Accounting.1


fmt_dollar() uses an f-string with , for thousands and .{digits}f for decimal places.

def fmt_dollar(x, digits=2):
    return f"${x:,.{digits}f}"

fmt_pct() takes a decimal rate, multiplies by 100, and formats the result.

def fmt_pct(x, digits=1):
    return f"{x * 100:.{digits}f}%"

Utility functions like fmt_pct() can be re-used in other, more complex functions.

print(fmt_dollar(9200))
#> $9,200.00
print(fmt_dollar(4200.50))
#> $4,200.50
print(fmt_pct(0.07))
#> 7.0%
print(fmt_pct(0.456))
#> 45.6%



fmt_dollar() adds a dollar sign, comma separators, and rounds to a set number of decimal places.

fmt_dollar <- function(x, digits = 2) {
  paste0("$", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits, big.mark = ","))
}

fmt_pct() expects a decimal rate (e.g. 0.07 for 7%) and converts it to a percentage string.

fmt_pct <- function(x, digits = 1) {
  paste0(round(x * 100, digits), "%")
}

This can be used to format percentages as strings with a percent sign.

fmt_dollar(9200)
#> [1] "$9,200.00"
fmt_dollar(4200.50)
#> [1] "$4,200.50"
fmt_pct(0.07)
#> [1] "7%"
fmt_pct(0.456)
#> [1] "45.6%"




Both fmt_dollar() and fmt_pct() follow the same convention: input is always a plain number, output is always a string. They are used throughout the remaining sections to clean up results.

The Wealth Formula
Galloway’s formula becomes real numbers when we picture someone earning $62,400 a year (about the 2025 median for full time workers). They save 15% ($9,360) every year and earn 8%. Each bar below is their savings at a checkpoint, split into what they put in and what it grew into.
Formula: Wealth after n years = Yearly savings × [((1 + r)^n − 1) ÷ r]
Yearly savings = Income × Savings rate, r is the yearly return, and n is the number of years.





$9,360 saved every year at 8%: money put in vs. growth







$9,360 saved every year at 8%: money put in vs. growth




The blue layer grows in a straight line, one $9,360 deposit per year. The green layer is growth, and it passes the blue layer after about year 18.

text:
Fixed-Cost Ratio
Fixed costs (rent, loan payments, insurance, utilities) are the bills you can’t easily change month to month. Picture a first job with $3,200 of take-home pay a month and $1,760 of fixed costs. The bar below cuts that paycheck into 10 equal pieces of $320 (each piece is 10%).
Formula: Fixed-Cost Ratio = Fixed Costs ÷ Take-Home Pay × 100





$3,200 take-home pay in 10 units of $320: fixed costs vs. flexible spending







$3,200 take-home pay in 10 units of $320: fixed costs vs. flexible spending




The red section covers 5 and a half of the 10 pieces, so fixed costs take 55% of the paycheck. The ceiling is 60% of $3,200, or $1,920.

title: Income
text:
Using Pipes in R
The pipe operator (|>) passes the output of one function directly into the next function as its first argument, so the code reads left to right instead of inside out. fixed_cost_ratio() already multiplies by 100, so we can pipe its result into round() and then paste0() to add the percent sign.
fixed_cost_ratio(fixed_costs = 1760, take_home = 3200) |> round(1) |> paste0("%")
Read that as: compute the ratio, then round it, then add the %. The version without a pipe nests the calls and reads from the inside out, which is harder to follow.
paste0(round(fixed_cost_ratio(fixed_costs = 1760, take_home = 3200), 1), "%")
When steps always belong together, wrap them in a single function so callers only see one name.

fixed_cost_pct <- function(fixed_costs, take_home) {
  fixed_cost_ratio(fixed_costs, take_home) |>
    round(1) |>
    paste0("%")
}


fixed_cost_pct(fixed_costs = 1760, take_home = 3200)
#> [1] "55%"

Python has no native pipe operator. The equivalent is storing the result from fixed_cost_ratio() in a variable and passing it to the next step:

def fixed_cost_pct(fixed_costs, take_home):
    ratio = fixed_cost_ratio(fixed_costs, take_home)
    return f"{ratio:.1f}%"


fixed_cost_pct(fixed_costs=1760, take_home=3200)
#> '55.0%'

Python’s approach emphasizes explicit intermediate steps. This reads top to bottom and makes debugging easier since you can inspect ratio along the way.
Read more about the pipe operator in R vs. Python.

What a Raise Is Really Worth
Say a raise adds $400 a month to your take-home pay, and you split it: $200 goes to your lifestyle and $200 gets invested. The chart shows what that single habit produces at 7% over 25 years.
Formula: FV = PMT × [((1 + r)^n − 1) ÷ r]
PMT is the amount invested each month, r is the monthly return (7% ÷ 12), and n is the number of months (25 × 12 = 300).

title: Financial Goals
text:
Book Topics

Short, medium, and long goals: when you need the money decides where it lives; under 3 years in high yield savings, 3 to 10 years in savings or a bond and stock mix, over 10 years in index funds inside retirement accounts
Wish vs. goal: a goal has a number, a date, and a monthly amount; give each goal its own named savings account and automate the transfer on payday
Do you need a goal to save?: Sethi and Preston give planned expenses their own step; Housel says savings with no goal attached buys flexibility; most people do best with both
How much to save: Sethi (about 10% of take home pay for investing plus 5% to 10% for goals), The Money Guy Show (25% of gross), 15% for retirement as a starting point; start with what you can and raise it with every raise
Sequencing goals: finish the Financial Order of Operations first, then fund goals one at a time or all at once; the last goal finishes on the same day either way
Tracking progress: check transfers monthly, compare balances every few months, add up net worth once a year, and notice when you hit a goal

title: Financial Goals
section: One Goal at a Time vs. All at Once
text:
One Goal at a Time vs. All at Once
When several goals share one monthly savings amount, the order changes when the first goal finishes. It never changes when the last one finishes.
Formula: Months to finish all goals = Total of all goals ÷ Monthly savings; Months to finish the first goal = First goal ÷ Amount going to it each month





Two goals funded with $600/month: one at a time vs. split evenly







Two goals funded with $600/month: one at a time vs. split evenly




Example: with $600 a month for a $3,000 trip and a $9,000 car, both goals are done in ($3,000 + $9,000) ÷ $600 = 20 months either way. The trip takes 5 months one at a time, or 10 months split evenly.
How to read this result: the order is a choice about which goal you want first, not about saving time overall. Put a fixed date goal (a wedding, a car on its last legs) first, or give it the bigger share.

title: Emergency Fund
text:
Book Topics

What it is: cash set aside for the unexpected so you never reach for credit; the target is 3 to 6 months of essential expenses, and it is Step 4 of the Financial Order of Operations
Why it matters: most derailments start with one surprise bill charged at 20 to 24% interest; Housel frames the fund as buying options, not earning a return
Essential expenses baseline: housing, groceries, utilities, transportation, health, and minimum debt payments; dining out and subscriptions do not count
Adjusting for risk: stable income with good coverage needs 3 to 4 months; dependents need 6 minimum; variable or self-employed income leans toward 6 to 9
Starter fund first: build $1,000, clear high-interest debt, then fill the full 3 to 6 month fund
Where to keep it: a high-yield savings account, money market fund, or insured credit union; not checking, stocks, long-term CDs, or cash at home
Why not the stock market: job losses and market drops tend to arrive together; Felix treats the fund as a hedge on human capital
Building it: 12 to 24 months is typical; doubling the contribution roughly halves the time; automate a payday transfer and find money in small cuts
Rebuilding: a withdrawal is the fund doing its job; resume contributions immediately without pausing retirement savings
Emergency fund math: target amount, months to reach the target, contribution needed by a deadline, and what the fund earns while you build it

title: Emergency Fund
text:
Your Target Amount
Your target is your essential monthly expenses multiplied by the number of months you want to cover. Each extra month adds one more block of expenses.
Formula: Target = Monthly Essential Expenses × Months of Coverage

text:
Months to Reach Your Target
Given your current balance and a monthly contribution, how long until you reach the target? Part of the target bar is already filled; the monthly contributions close the gap.
Formula: Months to Goal = (Target − Current Balance) ÷ Monthly Contribution
Book example: a $14,000 target with $2,000 saved and $500/month takes (14,000 − 2,000) ÷ 500 = 24 months.

A $14,000 target with $2,000 saved: the $12,000 gap, filled $500 at a time

text:
What the Fund Earns While You Build It
A fund in a high-yield savings account earns interest. It will not change your timeline much, but it is real money. Each month the balance is multiplied by (1 + the monthly rate).
Formula: Future Value = Balance × (1 + monthly rate)^months, where monthly rate = annual rate ÷ 12
Book example: $14,000 at 4.5%, untouched for 12 months, grows to about $14,643.





$14,000 at 4.5% for 12 months: your balance plus interest







$14,000 at 4.5% for 12 months: your balance plus interest

TipHow these exercises work



Each topic starts with a real scenario and a bar model, then three levels of exercises. Level 1 (Guided) fills in the blanks of a finished function. Level 2 (Practice) applies it to new numbers. title: Automating Savings
text:
Book Topics

Why automation matters: willpower is finite; save first and spend what remains (Sethi’s Conscious Spending Plan)
Money flow: split each paycheck on the first business day into savings, retirement, and checking
Method 1, direct deposit split: the cleanest approach; savings leave the paycheck before it reaches checking
Method 2, automatic bank transfers: the fallback; schedule a recurring transfer for the day after payday, never on payday itself
Pay yourself first math: Monthly Savings = Gross Monthly Income × Savings Rate, often split across an emergency fund, 401(k) match, sinking funds, and investing
Escalation: save half of every raise (Save More Tomorrow); stepping from 15% to 30% over seven years roughly doubles where you end up
Troubleshooting: lower the amount if you keep pulling money back; automate a percentage of average income if pay varies

title: Automating Savings
Automating Savings
text:
Direct Deposit Split
The book’s Method 1 example: a $5,000 gross paycheck, a 25% savings goal, a 10% 401(k) contribution taken before taxes, and about $750 in taxes. The 401(k) already covers part of the goal, so the HYSA only needs the rest.
Formula: HYSA Split = (Gross × Savings Rate) − 401(k); Checking Split = Gross − 401(k) − Taxes − HYSA Split
Example: 401(k) = $500, so the HYSA split is $1,250 − $500 = $750. The deposit is $5,000 − $500 − $750 = $3,750, and checking gets $3,750 − $750 = $3,000.





Where a $5,000 gross paycheck goes with a direct deposit split







Where a $5,000 gross paycheck goes with a direct deposit split




How to read this result: the HYSA and checking numbers are what you type into your payroll portal. The 401(k) and taxes are handled by payroll before the deposit.

  data.frame(k401, taxes, deposit, hysa, checking)

title: Automating Savings
text:
Escalating with Raises
Save half of every raise. Your spending still grows a little, and your savings rate climbs without a budget cut.
Formula: Extra Monthly Savings = (New Income − Old Income) × 0.5 ÷ 12; 30 Year Value = Monthly × ((1 + r/12)^360 − 1) ÷ (r/12)
Example: a raise from $50,000 to $52,000 adds $1,000 a year ($83.33 a month) to savings. In the book’s escalation table, $625 a month at 7% for 30 years grows to about $762k, and $1,575 a month grows to about $1.92M.





30 years of saving each year’s monthly amount at a 7% return







30 years of saving each year’s monthly amount at a 7% return




How to read this result: each step up in the savings rate adds hundreds of thousands of dollars after 30 years. The raises pay for it, so the money you live on never shrinks.

title: Asset Allocation
text:
Book Topics

Stocks, bonds, and cash: stocks grow most but can drop 30% to 50%; bonds grow slower and fall less; cash is the emergency fund and sits outside the investment split
How much in stocks when you’re young: everyone agrees on mostly stocks; Bogle (roughly your age in bonds, later 80 to 85% stocks), Sethi (80 to 90%), Collins (100% while building), Felix on the Cederburg research (100% stocks, global), Housel (extra cash for peace of mind); 80 to 90% is a reasonable start
US vs. international: 60/40 to 80/20 (US/international) is common; the Cederburg research goes to about one third US
Target date funds: one fund that sets the split and follows a glide path toward bonds; check the fee and don’t mix it with other funds
The three fund portfolio: total US stocks, total international stocks, total US bonds for about 0.05% (for example 60/30/10)
Rebalancing: check once a year and act when any part drifts more than about 5 percentage points; send new money to whatever is below target

title: Asset Allocation
text:
Good Years and Bad Years
A portfolio’s return is a weighted average of what each part earns.
Formula: Portfolio return = (Stock % × Stock return) + (Bond % × Bond return)
Example (stocks +10% average, −40% bad; bonds +4% average, 0% bad): an 80/20 split in a bad year is (0.80 × −40%) + (0.20 × 0%) = −32%, or −$3,200 on $10,000. In an average year it’s (0.80 × 10%) + (0.20 × 4%) = 8.8%, or +$880.





$10,000 in an average year and a bad year, by stock/bond split







$10,000 in an average year and a bad year, by stock/bond split




The second example adds more splits and two columns compared with 100/0: the average year gain you give up and the bad year loss you avoid. The third uses the real 2008 numbers from the book (stocks about −37%, bonds about +5%), where bonds actually went up.
Read the two columns together. Going from 100/0 to 60/40 gives up $240 in an average year but cuts the bad year loss from $4,000 to $2,400. Each step toward bonds trades a little growth for a softer fall.

title: Asset Allocation
section: How Much to Move When You Rebalance
text:
How Much to Move When You Rebalance
When one part grows or shrinks, move just enough to get back to the target split.
Formula: Amount to move = (Target % × Total) − Current amount
Example: $10,000 at 80/20, then stocks drop 30%. Stocks are $5,600, bonds $2,000, total $7,600 (stocks about 74%). (0.80 × $7,600) − $5,600 = $480 moved from bonds into stocks.





An 80/20 portfolio before a 30% stock drop, after it, and after rebalancing







An 80/20 portfolio before a 30% stock drop, after it, and after rebalancing




The second example runs several stock moves, up and down, and applies the book’s 5 percentage point rule to decide whether to act at all. A negative amount means sell stocks and buy bonds. The last example rebalances with new money only, so nothing gets sold.
Read a positive answer as “buy that much stock,” and a negative answer as “sell that much stock.” A 10% drop only moves the split about 2 points, so the 5 point rule says wait. With $1,000 of new money after the 30% drop, the full $1,000 goes to stocks and the gap closes from $480 to under $300 without selling anything.

text:
Book Topics

Mindset shift: a budget is intentional allocation, not restriction; reframe “I have to spend” as “my needs cost”; room for error is the most underrated concept (Housel)
Expense categories: fixed (lock in and automate), variable (category limits, not line by line tracking), periodic (set aside 1/12 of the annual cost each month)
Sinking funds: $1,200/year car insurance becomes $100/month; gifts $600 → $50, car maintenance $1,200 → $100, vacation $2,400 → $200
Zero-based budgeting: every dollar of a $5,000 paycheck gets a job and the remainder is $0; best for anyone rebuilding from debt or with irregular income
Percentage-based budgeting: Sethi’s Conscious Spending Plan (fixed 50 to 60%, investments 10%+, savings 5 to 10%, guilt-free 20 to 35%) next to the 50/30/20 rule
Recommendation: zero-based for 2 to 3 months, then graduate to percentages with automation
Tools: a spreadsheet with tabs for income, fixed, variable, sinking funds, net worth, and a summary; the best tool is the one you will actually use
Budgeting math: percentages, annualizing and monthly-izing, opportunity cost, break-even
Financial Order of Operations: the budget shows how much is left over; Preston’s FOO shows where it goes next

title: Budgeting
text:
Percentages
The foundational budgeting calculation: what share of income does each expense represent? Picture income as one bar and each expense as a slice of it.
Formula: (Expense ÷ Income) × 100
Book example: rent of $1,500 on $5,000 of take-home pay is 30% of income.





Rent ($1,500) as a share of a $5,000 paycheck







Rent ($1,500) as a share of a $5,000 paycheck





Level 1: Guided
Fill in the blanks to finish percent_of_income(), then find what share of a $5,000 paycheck goes to $1,500 of rent.

ExcelPythonR


With the expense in B2 (1500) and income in C2 (5000), write the percentage in D2.






NoteSolution





=(B2 / C2) * 100
This returns 30. Or enter =B2 / C2 and format the cell as a Percentage.











#| exercise: pct_1_py
def percent_of_income(expense, income):
    return (______ / ______) * 100

percent_of_income(1500, 5000)


The share is the part (the expense) divided by the whole (income).


Solution. 
def percent_of_income(expense, income):
    return (expense / income) * 100

percent_of_income(1500, 5000)


#| exercise: pct_1_py
#| check: true
if result is not None and abs(result - 30) < 0.01:
    feedback = {"correct": True, "message": "Right: rent is 30% of take-home pay."}
else:
    feedback = {"correct": False, "message": "Not quite. Divide the expense by income."}
feedback




#| exercise: pct_1_r
percent_of_income <- function(expense, income) {
  (______ / ______) * 100
}
percent_of_income(1500, 5000)


The share is the part (the expense) divided by the whole (income).


Solution. 
percent_of_income <- function(expense, income) {
  (expense / income) * 100
}
percent_of_income(1500, 5000)


#| exercise: pct_1_r
#| check: true
if (isTRUE(all.equal(.result, 30))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Right: rent is 30% of take-home pay.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Not quite. Divide the expense by income.")
}






Level 2: Practice
Here is the book’s zero-based budget for a $5,000 paycheck. What percent of income goes to Investments and Savings combined?



Category
Amount




Rent
$1,500


Groceries
$500


Transport
$300


Investments
$1,000


Savings
$500


Fun Money
$700


Other
$500




ExcelPythonR


Put categories in A2:A8, amounts in B2:B8, and income in E1. Find the combined percentage for Investments and Savings.






NoteSolution





In C2, lock the income cell with $ and fill down to C8:
=B2 / $E$1 * 100
Then add the two rows: =C5 + C6. The answer is 30.






#| exercise: pct_2_py
#| setup: true
import pandas as pd
def percent_of_income(expense, income):
    return (expense / income) * 100

budget = pd.DataFrame({
    "category": ["Rent", "Groceries", "Transport", "Investments",
                 "Savings", "Fun Money", "Other"],
    "amount": [1500, 500, 300, 1000, 500, 700, 500]
})


#| exercise: pct_2_py
budget["pct"] = percent_of_income(budget["amount"], 5000)
budget.loc[budget["category"].isin(______), "pct"].sum()


isin() takes a list: ["Investments", "Savings"].


Solution. 
budget["pct"] = percent_of_income(budget["amount"], 5000)
budget.loc[budget["category"].isin(["Investments", "Savings"]), "pct"].sum()


#| exercise: pct_2_py
#| check: true
if result is not None and abs(result - 30) < 0.01:
    feedback = {"correct": True, "message": "Right: 30% of income goes to your future self."}
else:
    feedback = {"correct": False, "message": "Not quite. Keep only Investments and Savings, then add their percentages."}
feedback




#| exercise: pct_2_r
#| setup: true
library(dplyr)
percent_of_income <- function(expense, income) {
  (expense / income) * 100
}
budget <- data.frame(
  category = c("Rent", "Groceries", "Transport", "Investments",
               "Savings", "Fun Money", "Other"),
  amount   = c(1500, 500, 300, 1000, 500, 700, 500)
)


#| exercise: pct_2_r
budget |>
  mutate(pct = percent_of_income(amount, 5000)) |>
  filter(category %in% ______) |>
  summarise(total = sum(pct)) |>
  pull(total)


%in% takes a vector: c("Investments", "Savings").


Solution. 
budget |>
  mutate(pct = percent_of_income(amount, 5000)) |>
  filter(category %in% c("Investments", "Savings")) |>
  summarise(total = sum(pct)) |>
  pull(total)


#| exercise: pct_2_r
#| check: true
if (isTRUE(all.equal(.result, 30))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Right: 30% of income goes to your future self.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Not quite. Keep only Investments and Savings, then add their percentages.")
}






Level 3: Challenge
Rent goes up from $1,500 to $1,800. To keep the budget zero-based (every dollar still adds up to $5,000), you take the extra $300 out of Fun Money. What percent of income is Fun Money now?

ExcelPythonR


Change the rent amount in B2, then change B7 (Fun Money) so B9 (the total) is still 5,000.






NoteSolution





Set B2 to 1800 and B7 to =700 - (B2 - 1500), which is 400. C7 then shows 8, and C9 still reads 100.






#| exercise: pct_3_py
#| setup: true
import pandas as pd
def percent_of_income(expense, income):
    return (expense / income) * 100

budget = pd.DataFrame({
    "category": ["Rent", "Groceries", "Transport", "Investments",
                 "Savings", "Fun Money", "Other"],
    "amount": [1500, 500, 300, 1000, 500, 700, 500]
})


#| exercise: pct_3_py
# raise rent, cut Fun Money by the same amount, and return Fun Money's percent



Change a single cell with budget.loc[budget["category"] == "Rent", "amount"] = 1800. Check that budget["amount"].sum() is still 5000.


Solution. 
budget.loc[budget["category"] == "Rent", "amount"] = 1800
budget.loc[budget["category"] == "Fun Money", "amount"] -= 300
fun = budget.loc[budget["category"] == "Fun Money", "amount"].sum()
percent_of_income(fun, 5000)


#| exercise: pct_3_py
#| check: true
if result is not None and abs(result - 8) < 0.01:
    feedback = {"correct": True, "message": "Right: Fun Money drops from 14% to 8%. Rent increases hit somewhere."}
else:
    feedback = {"correct": False, "message": "Not quite. Fun Money should fall from $700 to $400."}
feedback




#| exercise: pct_3_r
#| setup: true
library(dplyr)
percent_of_income <- function(expense, income) {
  (expense / income) * 100
}
budget <- data.frame(
  category = c("Rent", "Groceries", "Transport", "Investments",
               "Savings", "Fun Money", "Other"),
  amount   = c(1500, 500, 300, 1000, 500, 700, 500)
)


#| exercise: pct_3_r
# raise rent, cut Fun Money by the same amount, and return Fun Money's percent



Inside mutate(), use case_when() to change only the Rent and Fun Money rows, and .default = amount to keep the rest. Check that sum(amount) is still 5000.


Solution. 
budget |>
  mutate(amount = case_when(
    category == "Rent" ~ 1800,
    category == "Fun Money" ~ amount - 300,
    .default = amount
  )) |>
  filter(category == "Fun Money") |>
  mutate(pct = percent_of_income(amount, 5000)) |>
  pull(pct)


#| exercise: pct_3_r
#| check: true
if (isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(.result), 8))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Right: Fun Money drops from 14% to 8%. Rent increases hit somewhere.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Not quite. Fun Money should fall from $700 to $400.")
}

title: Budgeting
Budgeting
text:
Opportunity Cost
Every dollar spent is also what that dollar could have become. The hidden cost of any purchase is its future value if invested instead.
Formula: amount × (1 + r)^n
Book example: choosing a $15,000 used car over a $40,000 new one and investing the $25,000 difference at 7% for 30 years gives $25,000 × (1.07)^30 ≈ $190,000.





$25,000 invested at 7%: value at each checkpoint







$25,000 invested at 7%: value at each checkpoint





Level 1: Guided
Fill in the blanks to finish opportunity_cost(), then find what the $25,000 saved on a used car grows to in 30 years at 7%.

ExcelPythonR


Put the amount in A2 (25000), the rate in B2 (0.07), and years in C2 (30). Find the future value in D2.






NoteSolution





=A2*(1+B2)^C2
This returns $190,306.38.











#| exercise: opp_1_py
def opportunity_cost(amount, rate, years):
    return amount * (1 + ______) ** ______

opportunity_cost(25000, 0.07, 30)


Grow by (1 + rate) once for every year.


Solution. 
def opportunity_cost(amount, rate, years):
    return amount * (1 + rate) ** years

opportunity_cost(25000, 0.07, 30)


#| exercise: opp_1_py
#| check: true
if result is not None and abs(result - 190306.38) < 0.01:
    feedback = {"correct": True, "message": "Right: about $190,000. That's the real price of the new car."}
else:
    feedback = {"correct": False, "message": "Not quite. Raise (1 + rate) to the number of years."}
feedback




#| exercise: opp_1_r
opportunity_cost <- function(amount, rate, years) {
  amount * (1 + ______)^______
}
opportunity_cost(25000, 0.07, 30)


Grow by (1 + rate) once for every year.


Solution. 
opportunity_cost <- function(amount, rate, years) {
  amount * (1 + rate)^years
}
opportunity_cost(25000, 0.07, 30)


#| exercise: opp_1_r
#| check: true
if (isTRUE(all.equal(.result, 190306.38, tolerance = 1e-6))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Right: about $190,000. That's the real price of the new car.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Not quite. Raise (1 + rate) to the number of years.")
}

Level 3: Challenge
At 7%, how many whole years does it take for the $25,000 to double to $50,000?

ExcelPythonR


Put years 1 to 20 in A5:A24, find the value at each year in B, then find the first year at or above $50,000.






NoteSolution





In B5, then fill down:
=$A$2*(1+$B$2)^A5
Then =MATCH(TRUE, B5:B24>=50000, 0) returns 11. You can also solve it directly with =ROUNDUP(NPER(7%, 0, -25000, 50000), 0).

    return amount * (1 + rate) ** years


#| exercise: opp_3_py
years = 1
# keep adding a year until the value reaches $50,000

years


Use while opportunity_cost(25000, 0.07, years) < 50000: and add 1 to years inside the loop.


Solution.

while opportunity_cost(25000, 0.07, years) < 50000:
    years += 1

years

#| check: true
if result == 11:
    feedback = {"correct": True, "message": "Right: 11 years. The rule of 72 (72 / 7 = about 10.3) gets you close."}
else:

}

years <- 1:20

opportunity_cost() is vectorized, so pass all 20 years at once. Then use min(years[...]).

value <- opportunity_cost(25000, 0.07, years)
min(years[value >= 50000])
