title: Estate Planning
text:
Book Topics

Why it matters young: at 18 your parents lose the right to act for you; set up a plan while you’re thinking clearly, since people tend to miss their own cognitive decline
Beneficiary designations: the ten minute task; name a primary and contingent beneficiary on retirement plans, IRAs, HSAs, life insurance, and bank (POD) and brokerage (TOD) accounts; these forms override your will
Financial power of attorney: a durable POA names an agent to handle your money if you can’t
Healthcare directive and HIPAA release: a healthcare proxy and living will (often one advance directive), plus a HIPAA form so doctors can share information
Will and trust: a will covers what has no beneficiary, names an executor, and names a guardian for children; without one, state intestate succession decides; most people starting out don’t need a trust
Paperwork and parents: store originals safely, keep an account list (no passwords), set up password manager emergency access, and ask your parents about their plan

title: Estate Planning
section: What You Own and What You Owe
text:
What You Own and What You Owe
Your estate starts with your net worth: everything you own minus everything you owe.
Formula: Net worth = Total assets − Total debts





Assets, debts, and net worth for a 25 year old







Assets, debts, and net worth for a 25 year old




Example: ($12,000 + $6,000 + $8,000 + $9,000) − ($6,000 + $1,000) = $35,000 − $7,000 = a net worth of $28,000.
How to read this result: net worth is the yearly check in on your progress. It’s also roughly what your estate would be worth today, before adding any life insurance.

Level 1: Guided
Fill in the blanks to finish net_worth(), then find the net worth for assets of $12,000 (401(k)), $6,000 (Roth IRA), $8,000 (savings), and $9,000 (car), with debts of $6,000 (car loan) and $1,000 (credit card).

ExcelPythonR


Put the assets in B2:B5 and the debts in B7:B8. Find net worth in B10.






NoteSolution





=SUM(B2:B5) - SUM(B7:B8)
This returns $28,000.






#| exercise: nw_1_py
def net_worth(assets, debts):
    return ______(assets) - ______(debts)

net_worth([12000, 6000, 8000, 9000], [6000, 1000])


Add up everything you own, then everything you owe.


Solution. 
def net_worth(assets, debts):
    return sum(assets) - sum(debts)

net_worth([12000, 6000, 8000, 9000], [6000, 1000])


#| exercise: nw_1_py
#| check: true
if result is not None and abs(result - 28000) < 0.01:
    feedback = {"correct": True, "message": "Right: $35,000 owned minus $7,000 owed is $28,000."}
else:
    feedback = {"correct": False, "message": "Not quite. Total each side with sum()."}
feedback




#| exercise: nw_1_r
net_worth <- function(assets, debts) {
  ______(assets) - ______(debts)
}
net_worth(c(12000, 6000, 8000, 9000), c(6000, 1000))


Add up everything you own, then everything you owe.


Solution. 
net_worth <- function(assets, debts) {
  sum(assets) - sum(debts)
}
net_worth(c(12000, 6000, 8000, 9000), c(6000, 1000))


#| exercise: nw_1_r
#| check: true
if (isTRUE(abs(as.numeric(.result) - 28000) < 0.01)) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Right: $35,000 owned minus $7,000 owed is $28,000.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Not quite. Total each side with sum().")
}

title: High-Yield Savings Accounts
text:
Book Topics

Separate account: the real benefit of a savings account at a different bank is friction; 1 to 2 days to move money back stops impulse spending
Choosing an account: need it within 6 months? Use a HYSA. Can you lock it away for 3 to 60 months? Consider a CD
Comparing HYSAs: online banks pay about 4 to 5% APY and differ by only 0.1 to 0.4%; all of them beat the 0.01% at traditional banks by about 400×
APY vs. APR: APY already includes daily compounding, so balance growth is Starting Balance × (1 + APY)^years
FDIC insurance: covers up to $250,000 per account holder per bank; money market accounts are a close alternative with possible withdrawal limits
Savings hierarchy: emergency fund, sinking funds, and short term goals go in a HYSA; 3 to 5 year goals in CDs or short term bonds; 5+ years goes to investing

title: High-Yield Savings Accounts
text:
HYSA Balance
APY is the total return for a year with compounding already included. To grow a balance, multiply by (1 + APY) once for each year you hold the money.
Formula: Ending Balance = Starting Balance × (1 + APY)^years
(The daily math belongs to the APR: APY = (1 + APR ÷ 365)^365 − 1.)
Example: $10,000 at 4.35% APY grows to $10,000 × 1.0435 = $10,435 after one year ($435 in interest) and to $12,373 after five years.





$10,000 at 4.35% APY: deposit and interest earned, year by year







$10,000 at 4.35% APY: deposit and interest earned, year by year




How to read this result: the green layer is money the bank paid you. On $10,000 the gap between online banks is about $20 a year, but the gap between any of them and a traditional bank is over $400.

title: High-Yield Savings Accounts
text:
Small Rate Gaps Over Time
The book says a 0.3% difference looks like noise at first but adds up over 30 years of regular deposits. To check, we need the growth of a monthly deposit, using the monthly rate that matches the APY.
Formula: Future Value = Deposit × ((1 + i)^(12 × years) − 1) ÷ i, where i = (1 + APY)^(1/12) − 1
Example: $500 a month for 30 years grows to about $342,635 at 4.0% APY and $360,801 at 4.3% APY, a gap of about $18,166.





$500 a month for 30 years at three APYs







$500 a month for 30 years at three APYs




How to read this result: the gap is small for the first few years and grows with time. It is worth picking a good rate once, but not worth switching banks every month to chase 0.05%.

title: High-Yield Savings Accounts
text:
FDIC Coverage
FDIC insurance covers up to $250,000 per account holder per bank. Anything above that at one bank is not insured.
Formula: Insured = smaller of (Balance, $250,000); Uninsured = Balance − Insured; Banks Needed = Balance ÷ $250,000, rounded up
Example: a $10,000 balance is fully insured. A $500,000 balance at one bank has $250,000 uninsured, so it needs two banks.
How to read this result: if the uninsured column is above zero, move that amount to an account at a different bank.

title: DEV (fm-finance)
text: This site holds the exercises for Personal Finance: a Field Manual. Reading about the math is a good start, but the formulas stick once you work through them with real numbers. Each page here matches a chapter in the book. It opens with Book Topics, a short summary of the chapter, and then turns each math topic into practice.

title: DEV (fm-finance)
text:
How the exercises work
Every math topic starts with a bar model (a picture of the numbers) and then three levels of exercises:

Level 1 (Guided): fill in the blanks of a finished formula.
Level 2 (Practice): use the same formula on new numbers.
Level 3 (Challenge): answer a new question with less help.

Each level has Excel, Python, and R tabs. Excel is included because it’s used in just about every organization, so it’s the tool you’re most likely to have at work. R and Python are included because both are open source (and free), so anyone can use them. You don’t have to learn all three; pick the tab that fits the tool you use now (or the one you want to learn).
The R and Python exercises run right in your browser, so you can try them without installing anything. Click Run Code to try an answer and Submit Answer to check it. If you get stuck, the hint and solution are there. The Excel exercises have a solution you can reveal.

title: Insurance
text:
Book Topics

The rule: insure losses you can’t absorb; cover small ones from your emergency fund (leave room for error)
Insurance words: premium, deductible, claim, coverage limit, liability; premiums and deductibles move in opposite directions
Health insurance: never go without; stay on a parent’s plan until 26, get it through work, or use the marketplace; copay, coinsurance, and the out of pocket maximum (your worst case, capped at $10,600 in 2026); high deductible plans qualify for an HSA with a deductible of at least $1,700 and an out of pocket maximum of no more than $8,500
Auto insurance: liability of at least 100/300/100; consider dropping collision and comprehensive on a cheap car
Renters insurance: about $13 to $23 a month; choose replacement cost over actual cash value
Disability insurance: about 1 in 4 of today’s 20 year olds will become disabled before retirement age; take employer long term disability (about 60% of pay)
Life insurance: only if someone depends on your income; buy term, about 10 times yearly income; skip whole life
Umbrella insurance: $1 million or more of extra liability; revisit as net worth grows
What to skip: extended warranties, phone insurance, life insurance with no dependents, single event policies

title: Insurance
text:
Choosing a Deductible
A higher deductible lowers your premium but costs more on each claim. The break even point is how many years of premium savings it takes to cover the extra deductible.
Formula: Break even years = (Higher deductible − Lower deductible) ÷ Yearly premium savings





Savings from a $1,000 deductible vs. a $500 deductible, year by year







Savings from a $1,000 deductible vs. a $500 deductible, year by year




Car insurance costs $1,500 a year with a $500 deductible, or $1,350 with a $1,000 deductible. ($1,000 − $500) ÷ $150 = about 3.3 years. If you file a claim less often than that, the higher deductible comes out ahead.
How to read this result: a positive yearly gain means the higher deductible saves money on average. The gain turns negative only if you claim more often than the break even. Either way, pick the higher deductible only if your emergency fund can cover it.

title: Insurance
text:
Comparing Two Health Plans
A health plan’s real yearly cost is its premiums plus your share of medical bills, minus any money your employer puts in your HSA. Your share can never go above the out of pocket maximum.
Formula: Yearly cost = (Monthly premium × 12) + min(Medical bills, Out of pocket max) − Employer HSA money
This simple version assumes you pay all medical bills up to the out of pocket maximum, so it slightly overstates plans with coinsurance.





Total yearly cost of two health plans in a healthy year and the worst year







Total yearly cost of two health plans in a healthy year and the worst year




Plan A has a $100 monthly premium and a $3,000 out of pocket maximum. Plan B has a $40 monthly premium, a $5,000 out of pocket maximum, and $500 a year from your employer in the HSA. In a healthy year ($300 of care), Plan A costs $1,500 and Plan B costs $280. In the worst year, Plan A costs $4,200 and Plan B costs $4,980.





Yearly cost of each plan as medical bills grow







Yearly cost of each plan as medical bills grow




How to read this result: the gap between the lines is what you save (or lose) with Plan B. Below $4,220 of bills, Plan B wins by up to $1,220. Above it, Plan A wins by at most $780. If you put Plan B’s savings into the HSA, one healthy year covers the difference.

This returns $1,500.

title: Major Purchases
text:
Book Topics

Renting vs. buying: “renting is throwing money away” is a myth; you pay for shelter either way, and Ben Felix’s research shows renting and investing the difference often matches or beats owning
True cost of owning: mortgage interest, property tax (1% to 2%), maintenance (about 1%), insurance, closing costs (3% to 5%), and the opportunity cost of the down payment
Felix’s 5% rule: unrecoverable costs run about 5% of home value per year (property tax ~1% + maintenance ~1% + cost of capital ~3%); divide by 12 and compare to rent
When to buy or rent: buy if you’ll stay 7+ years, have stable income and an emergency fund, and keep housing under 28% to 30% of gross income; rent if you may move within 5 to 7 years or need flexibility; a decision flowchart ties it together
Front loaded interest: on a 30 year mortgage at 6%, more than 80% of the first year’s payments go to interest, so moving every 5 years means barely touching principal

title: Major Purchases
text:
The Rent-vs-Buy 5% Rule
The 5% rule adds up three costs every owner pays and never gets back. Divide by 12 and you have a monthly rent to compare against.
Formula: Monthly cost of owning ≈ (Home Value × 0.05) ÷ 12





The three components of the 5% rule on a $500,000 home







The three components of the 5% rule on a $500,000 home




Example: a $500,000 home → (500,000 × 0.05) ÷ 12 = $2,083 a month. Rent below that, and renting and investing the difference tends to win.
How to read this result: the threshold is the rent at which renting and owning cost about the same. It’s a quick filter, not a final answer; your plans to stay and your local rents still matter.

The Monthly Mortgage Payment
The standard amortization formula spreads the loan plus all future interest into equal monthly payments. Shorter terms mean higher payments but far less total interest.
Formula: M = P × [r(1 + r)^n] ÷ [(1 + r)^n − 1], where P = loan principal, r = annual rate ÷ 12, n = years × 12





Monthly payment on a $480,000 loan at 6% across three terms







Monthly payment on a $480,000 loan at 6% across three terms




Example: a $480,000 loan (a $600,000 home with 20% down) at 6% for 30 years → about $2,878 a month.
How to read this result: the monthly payment is only part of the cost. Before choosing a term, check that the payment plus property tax and insurance stays under 28% to 30% of gross income.

title: Major Purchases
section: Where the First Year’s Payments Go
text:
Where the First Year’s Payments Go
In month one, interest is the balance times the monthly rate. Only what’s left over reduces the principal.
Formula: First month interest = Principal × (annual rate ÷ 12); First month principal = Monthly payment − First month interest





Interest vs. principal split at three points on a $480,000 / 6% / 30-yr mortgage







Interest vs. principal split at three points on a $480,000 / 6% / 30-yr mortgage




Example: on that $480,000 loan, month one interest is $2,400 of the $2,878 payment, about 83% interest, leaving only about $478 toward principal.
How to read this result: early on, your payment mostly rents money from the bank. Equity builds slowly at first and quickly at the end, so selling within a few years leaves little principal paid down.

Level 1: Guided

title: R vs. Python
text:
The sections below are a quick reference for the most important differences in syntax and style between R and Python. Don’t worry about memorizing these right now—just know that they exist, and you’ll see examples of each in the next chapters.





R uses <- (preferred convention) or = for assignment.


Python Uses = for assignment.






x <- 10


x = 10









R Functions are created with function() and assigned to a variable. Function bodies are wrapped in curly braces {}.


Python Functions are defined with the def keyword, followed by a colon and an indented body.






add_fun <- function(a, b) {
  a + b
}


def add_fun(a, b):
    return a + b









R automatically returns the last evaluated expression. The return() function is optional.


Python requires an explicit return statement to return a value—otherwise returns None.






double_fun <- function(x) x * 2


def double_fun(x):
    return x * 2









R has a built-in pipe |> (base R) and the popular %>% operator from magrittr/dplyr for chaining operations.


Python has no native pipe operator. Chaining is done via method calls—polars is especially well-suited for this style.






data |>
  filter(x > 5) |>
  summarise(avg = mean(x))


import polars as pl

(
    data
    .filter(pl.col("x") > 5)
    .select(pl.col("x").mean().alias("avg"))
)









R uses paste(), paste0(), sprintf(), or glue::glue() for string construction.


Python uses f-strings, the .format() method, or % formatting.






name <- "John"
paste0("Hello, ", name)
glue::glue("Hello, {name}")


name = "John"
f"Hello, {name}"









R uses curly braces {} to define code blocks. Indentation is purely stylistic.


Python uses indentation (typically 4 spaces) to define code blocks. Indentation is syntactically required.






if (x > 0) {
  print("positive")
}


if x > 0:
    print("positive")









Spaces, line breaks, and indentation are flexible and stylistic in R


In Python, indentation is syntactic (inconsistent indentation raises an IndentationError). Blank lines are ignored but can be used to separate code blocks for readability.






# R — all of this is valid 
# and produces the same result

# Clean, conventional style
if (x > 0) {
  result <- x * 2
  print(result)
}

# Messy but still valid
if(x>0){result<-x*2
    print(result)}

# Extreme and ugly but works
if   (  x > 0  )    {
result        <-x*2
   print(   result   )
              }


# Python — indentation matters
# Correct: consistent 4-space 
# indentation
if x > 0:
    result = x * 2
    print(result)

# Blank lines are fine 
# they improve readability
def process(x):

    if x > 0:
        result = x * 2

        print(result)

    return result

# Raises IndentationError
if x > 0:
    result = x * 2
        print(result) # ❌ bad indent









R uses 1-based indexing.


Python uses 0-based indexing.






vec <- c("a", "b", "c")
vec[1]   # returns "a"


lst = ["a", "b", "c"]
lst[0]   # returns "a"









R uses NA (with variants like NA_integer_, NA_character_), plus NULL and NaN.


Python uses None natively; polars represents missing values as null in its columnar data structures.






x <- c(1, NA, 3)
is.na(x)


import polars as pl
s = pl.Series([1, None, 3])
s.is_null()









In R, vectors are first-class citizens—most operations are vectorized by default.


In Python, native lists are not vectorized. Vector math requires numpy or columnar libraries like polars.






c(1, 2, 3) * 2   
# returns c(2, 4, 6)


import polars as pl
pl.Series([1, 2, 3]) * 2   
# returns Series [2, 4, 6]









In R, packages are installed with install.packages() and loaded with library().


In Python, packages are installed via pip or conda from the terminal and loaded with import.






install.packages("dplyr")
library(dplyr)


# terminal: pip install polars
import polars as pl









In R, comments are single-line only, using #. No multi-line comment syntax.


In Python, single-line comments use #. Triple-quoted strings ("""...""") are commonly used as block comments or docstrings.






# This is a comment


# This is a comment

"""
This is a multi-line
comment or docstring.
"""









In R, TRUE / FALSE (can be abbreviated as T / F).


In Python, True / False (capitalized, no abbreviation).






flag <- TRUE


flag = True






R uses &, |, ! for vectorized logic; &&, || for scalar logic.
c(TRUE, FALSE) & c(TRUE, TRUE)   # vectorized
TRUE && FALSE                    # scalar
Python uses and, or, not for scalar logic; &, |, ~ for vectorized logic in numpy/polars expressions.
True and False  # scalar

import polars as pl
df.filter((pl.col("a") > 0) & (pl.col("b") < 10)) # vectorized



data.frame is built into base R; enhanced versions include tibble (tidyverse) and data.table.
df <- data.frame(
    name = c("A", "B"), 
    value = c(1, 2)
  )
In Python, data frames are not built-in—requires a library like polars (pl.DataFrame), which offers fast, multithreaded performance and a clean expression API.
import polars as pl
df = pl.DataFrame({"name": ["A", "B"], "value": [1, 2]})

text:
TipHow these exercises work



Each topic starts with a real scenario and a bar model, then three levels of exercises. Level 1 (Guided) fills in the blanks of a finished function. Level 2 (Practice) applies it to new numbers. Level 3 (Challenge) asks a new question with little scaffolding. The R and Python exercises run in your browser: click Run Code to try, Submit Answer to check, and use the hint or solution if you get stuck. Excel exercises have a solution you can reveal.

title: Savings Strategies
text:
Book Topics

Savings rate: the one number to track; it sets the speed of wealth building more than income does (a $40,000 earner saving 40% reaches $500k in 18 years, a $120,000 earner saving 10% takes 21)
Benchmarks: under 10% danger zone; 10 to 20% average; 20 to 30% strong; 30%+ path to financial independence within a decade or two
Make savings automatic: automate transfers the day after payday, use a separate bank, label each account by purpose, and track progress visually
Savings and the FOO: saving shows up at nearly every step of the Financial Order of Operations; the right rate is the one you can keep up for decades
Account types: high yield savings and money market accounts for emergency and sinking funds, CDs for known future goals, regular savings to avoid
FDIC insurance: covers up to $250,000 per account holder per bank; spread larger balances across banks

title: Savings Strategies
text:
Savings Rate
The savings rate is the slice of your income bar that goes to savings. Every dollar goes to either spending or savings, so the rate measures how big the savings slice is.
Formula: Savings Rate = (Income − Spending) ÷ Income × 100
Example: you take home $5,000 and spend $3,500. (5,000 − 3,500) ÷ 5,000 = 30% savings rate.





Savings slice as a percentage of income (same $60k income, different rates)







Savings slice as a percentage of income (same $60k income, different rates)




How to read this result: a 30% rate means 30 cents of every dollar you bring home stays with you. If the rate is negative, you are spending more than you earn and the gap is coming from savings or debt.

Level 1: Guided
Fill in the blanks to finish savings_rate(), then find the savings rate when you take home $5,000 and spend $3,500.

ExcelPythonR


Put income in A2 (5000) and spending in B2 (3500). Find the savings rate in C2.






NoteSolution





=(A2 - B2) / A2 * 100
This returns 30.






#| exercise: rate_1_py
def savings_rate(income, spending):
    return ((______ - ______) / income) * 100

savings_rate(5000, 3500)


What you save is what you earn minus what you spend.


Solution. 
def savings_rate(income, spending):
    return ((income - spending) / income) * 100

savings_rate(5000, 3500)


#| exercise: rate_1_py
#| check: true
if result is not None and abs(result - 30) < 0.001:
    feedback = {"correct": True, "message": "Right: a 30% savings rate."}

feedback

title: Savings Strategies
text:
Years to a Savings Target
The book compares two savers at a 7% return. One earns $40,000 and saves 40% ($16,000 a year). The other earns $120,000 and saves 10% ($12,000 a year). The bigger saver reaches $500,000 first. We can solve for the number of years directly.
Formula: Years = ln(1 + Target × r ÷ Annual Savings) ÷ ln(1 + r)
Example: ln(1 + 500,000 × 0.07 ÷ 16,000) ÷ ln(1.07) = 17.1 years, so the balance passes $500k during year 18. At $12,000 a year it takes 20.2 years, so year 21.





Years to reach $500,000 at a 7% return on a $60,000 income







Years to reach $500,000 at a 7% return on a $60,000 income




How to read this result: the answer is the number of years of steady saving needed, not counting anything you already have. Raising the savings rate shortens the timeline much more at low rates than at high ones.

Fill in the blanks to finish years_to_target(), then find how long $16,000 a year at 7% takes to reach $500,000.

NoteSolution

This returns about 17.1 years.

title: Taxes
text:
Book Topics

Where your paycheck goes: withholding for federal income tax, Social Security (6.2%), Medicare (1.45%), and state tax; FICA (7.65%) starts at the first dollar (about $3,443 on $45,000); 401(k) contributions are your money, not a tax
Tax brackets: 2026 single filer brackets (10% to 37%); only dollars above each line get the higher rate, so a raise always leaves you with more; marginal rate vs. effective rate
Deductions vs. credits: the 2026 standard deduction is $16,100; credits cut tax dollar for dollar (Saver’s Credit up to $1,000 for income up to $40,250, American Opportunity, Earned Income)
The W-4 and your refund: a big refund is an interest free loan to the government; aim for a small refund or small bill; side income needs 25% to 30% set aside for taxes (self employment tax of about 15.3%)
Filing: due around April 15; IRS Free File, VITA, Free File Fillable Forms (Direct File is not available for 2026)
Tax loss harvesting: only matters in a taxable account, and mostly delays taxes rather than avoiding them
When to hire a pro: side income, rentals or a business, big life changes, IRS letters, large taxable sales

title: Taxes
section: Your Tax Bill, Bracket by Bracket
text:
Your Tax Bill, Bracket by Bracket
Each slice of taxable income is taxed at its own rate. The standard deduction comes off the top first, so those dollars are taxed at 0%.
Formula: Tax = Σ (Rate × Income in that bracket), and Effective rate = Tax ÷ Income





A $45,000 salary, sliced by the standard deduction and 2026 tax brackets







A $45,000 salary, sliced by the standard deduction and 2026 tax brackets




On $45,000, the tax is ($12,400 × 10%) + ($16,500 × 12%) = $3,220. That is an effective rate of about 7.2%, even though the top bracket is 12%.





Marginal rate (steps) vs. effective rate (smooth curve), 2026 single filer







Marginal rate (steps) vs. effective rate (smooth curve), 2026 single filer




How to read this result: the marginal rate tells you what happens to your next dollar. The effective rate tells you what share of your whole salary went to federal income tax. Use the marginal rate for decisions (like a Traditional 401(k) contribution) and the effective rate for budgeting.

Level 1: Guided
Fill in the blanks to finish income_tax() for a 2026 single filer (standard deduction $16,100), then find the federal income tax on a $45,000 salary.

ExcelPythonR


Put the salary in A2 (45000). The taxable income is the salary minus $16,100. Write the tax in B2 using the first three brackets (10% to $12,400, 12% to $50,400, 22% above).






NoteSolution





=LET(t, MAX(A2-16100, 0),
  0.10*MIN(t, 12400) + 0.12*MAX(MIN(t, 50400)-12400, 0) + 0.22*MAX(MIN(t, 105700)-50400, 0))
This returns $3,220.






#| exercise: bracket_1_py
def income_tax(income, deduction=16100):
    taxable = max(______ - deduction, 0)
    lower = [0, 12400, 50400, 105700, 201775, 256225, 640600]
    upper = lower[1:] + [float("inf")]
    rate = [0.10, 0.12, 0.22, 0.24, 0.32, 0.35, 0.37]
    return sum(r * max(min(taxable, u) - ______, 0) for r, l, u in zip(rate, lower, upper))

income_tax(45000)


Taxable income is what’s left after the deduction. In each bracket, tax only the part of taxable income above that bracket’s lower edge l.


Solution.

income_tax(45000)
